condensed.text: The narrator began his journalism career as a reporter for the Ram, the student newspaper at Fordham University in the Bronx.
One day the narrator walked toward the campus center and encountered Dean McGowan, who had architected a policy to replace working- and middle-class students with wealthier ones.
The narrator approached Dean McGowan with his notebook and asked whether Fordham planned to raise tuition substantially above inflation and whether that would betray its mission.
Dean McGowan stopped and called the narrator a punk, and then a figure appeared holding a cream pie and mashed it into Dean McGowan's face before running away.
The Dean stood covered in cream.
The narrator asked Dean McGowan to comment on the attack, and the Dean responded with an obscenity directed at the narrator.
The narrator raced back to the newsroom and found the editor Jim Dwyer, a senior who would later win a Pulitzer Prize.
The narrator pitched his story to Dwyer, who called Dean McGowan a dick and told the narrator to write it up.
The narrator wrote the story and knew it was good, then decided to improve it by adding embellishment.
Reporters call embellishment making things up and recommend against crossing that line.
The narrator had just witnessed the line crossed between a high-powered dean and assault with a pastry, and he liked it.
The narrator gave the figure the name Pie Man with capital letters and described him as a cape-wearing masked avenger, though he had actually been capeless.
The narrator wrote that Pie Man clicked his heels in rakish glee as he fled the scene.
The narrator gave Pie Man a Latin catchphrase, writing that he cried out a phrase meaning he was not an animal, which made no sense.
The narrator needed something, and Latin came naturally to him as a Catholic.
The narrator finished the story and handed it to Dwyer, who read it and expressed enthusiasm for Pie Man and assigned it to page one.
That was how the first line got crossed.
A few days later the narrator received a letter praising his story and its details.
The letter invited him to be on the steps of Duane Library Tuesday at 3 o'clock to see Pie Man in action again, and Pie Man signed it.
The narrator arrived at the location with a photographer from the Ram.
Sheila Beale, the student-body president, came out of the library.
Sheila differed from the narrator and other Fordham students who wore flannel shirts and worked part-time jobs.
Sheila was well-bred, had school spirit, and was the kind of student Dean McGowan wanted more of.
Rumor suggested Dean McGowan had an intimate relationship with Sheila in his office, though the narrator acknowledged this as unverified.
Sheila had collaborated with the Dean to ban outdoor drinking on campus, the infamous no-beer-at-barbecues rule.
The narrator acknowledged audience disapproval of the rule.
Sheila considered public drinking to be in poor taste.
The narrator indicated the audience knew what happened next.
Pie Man emerged from behind the late-night library drop-box, hit Sheila with a pie, and fled while crying his Latin catchphrase, according to the narrator's story in the newspaper the next day.
The newspaper ran a photo of Pie Man leaving the scene with a cape flowing behind him while making a gesture.
The coverage made Pie Man a sensation on campus, and people started dressing like him and quoting him in class.
The Ram ran five major stories about Pie Man, all written by the narrator.
Toward the end of this run, the narrator went to a bar one night and saw Angela from his British Literature class drinking with friends.
The narrator and Angela had been flirting for two months, though the narrator had been doing the flirting with such subtlety that Angela might not have known he existed.
The narrator saw Angela and made a mental note to do nothing about it.
The narrator went to the bar to buy a round and felt a tap on his shoulder from Angela.
Angela told Jim that she and others had noticed he always seemed to know when and where Pie Man would strike.
Angela asked Jim if he was Pie Man.
Jim recognized that if he said yes, Angela would have sex with him.
Jim considered whether he was really Pie Man for having brought the character into being and for being Angela's only source of knowledge about Pie Man.
Angela had asked Jim a straightforward question that required a straightforward answer.
Jim was not actually Pie Man and had never seen the person out of costume.
Jim told Angela that he was Pie Man.
Angela expressed approval and asked Jim to buy her a beer and tell her all about it.
